name: HH-suite (hhsearch)
kind: builds a profile of a protein family
compares: Two profiles against each other. Here each profile was built from a single protein, not from a family alignment, because no UniRef30 database was given.
reference: Single-protein profiles of the relative's proteome (Quest for Orthologs reference proteomes, release 2020_04), as an HH-suite database.
score: Bit score from hhsearch: higher ranks first.
caveats: The run names this tool hhblits (its tool id), but it ran hhsearch on profiles of single proteins. HH-suite's usual use, with family alignments from UniRef30, was not run, so these numbers say nothing about it.

known_failure_modes.finding: Aligner calls run past the domain, because a call spans the whole aligned stretch. Over correct calls, they start a median 5 to 21 residues early. Over all calls, 45% to 60% start more than 100 residues early.
known_failure_modes.number: median 5 to 21 residues early; 45% to 60% more than 100 residues early

evidence.quote: Over correct calls, the median of call start minus true start is 0 for hmmscan, whose models define the Pfam truth, so the 1-based reading of truth and aligners holds. Aligners start a median 5 to 21 residues early, because a call spans the whole aligned stretch.
45% to 60% of aligner calls start more than 100 residues early, not "most"

known_failure_modes.run: `make leaderboard-pileup` and the region pile-up page (Figure 4)
known_failure_modes.what_to_do: Read a call's ends as the alignment's ends, not the domain's. To score where a domain sits, place the target's domain through the alignment.

commercial_use: Yes. If you distribute a changed version, you must release its source under GPL-3.0 too.
command:
ffindex_apply \
    human-38fdd87d_hhdb/db_a3m.ffdata human-38fdd87d_hhdb/db_a3m.ffindex \
    -d results.ffdata -i results.ffindex \
    -- hhsearch -i stdin -d zebrafish_hhdb/db -blasttab /dev/stdout -cpu 16 -v 0
questions: Is the closest same-family domain in the relative you will search at least 40% identical, for most of your proteins? If yes, Fmax here is 40–60% 0.248 (n = 563), 60–100% 0.283 (n = 1,289). If no, 20–30% 0.321 (n = 93), 30–40% 0.190 (n = 165). (Pfam truth set, raw calls, zebrafish (435 Mya) as the relative searched, setting single-protein profiles; subsets with at least 30 true instances.)

Are the features you care about longer than 60 residues? If yes, Fmax here is 61–120 aa 0.230 (n = 963), 121–250 aa 0.298 (n = 504), 251 aa or more 0.417 (n = 277). If no, 16–30 aa 0.066 (n = 271), 31–60 aa 0.085 (n = 420). (Pfam truth set, raw calls, zebrafish (435 Mya) as the relative searched, setting single-protein profiles.)
Can you spend about 24.8 core-hours per 1,000 proteins for each relative you search? That is the measured mean per relative; see "Cost per 1,000 queries" below.
